summary: A 1970 proposal by M. Elie for a Network Interchange Language, a common way for different computers to exchange information. It is an early proposal in the series, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 51 proposes a Network Interchange Language (NIL) for programs on different computers to exchange data. It describes a shared Network Machine model and host-specific translators that would convert data to and from that model.

subtitle: An early proposal for a common language for exchanging data across the ARPA network.

tldr.problem: Different hosts may represent data and describe their environments in different ways, making program communication across the network difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed Network Interchange Language uses an abstract Network Machine, with sublanguages for control, operations, data declarations, and environment descriptions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 51 is a proposal. It describes a generator on each host that would create a translator between the host's data format and the Network Machine format.

today: RFC 51 is an early proposal, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown with no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The memo describes NIL as a proposal and does not state that it was adopted.

sections.title: A Common Language for Network Programs
sections.content:
RFC 51 proposes a high-level programming language for computer networks, especially the ARPA network. Its central concept is an abstract Network Machine: a host communicates with this machine using the same language, while the machine's configuration may vary with the remote host.

The proposal aims to describe a program's environment, including data formats and structures, input and output devices, and operating-system interfaces. It also aims to express the front end of an interactive system while limiting the effect of transmission delay on response time.
sections.plainLanguage: NIL proposes a shared way for programs on different hosts to describe data and communicate. A Network Machine provides the common model that each host uses.

sections.title: Four Sublanguages and the Network Machine
sections.content:
NIL is divided into a control sublanguage for the order and location of computations, an operation sublanguage for actions on data, a data declaration sublanguage for variables and structures, and an environment sublanguage for the program's operating context. A complete program descriptor contains an environment section, a data declaration section, a control section, and an operation section.

The abstract Network Machine is described as having infinite memory and variable word length. It can use a standard mode with predefined data elements and structures, or an extended mode in which a host defines additional elements, structures, and transformations.
sections.plainLanguage: NIL has separate parts for describing data, operations, control flow, and the program's environment. The proposed Network Machine can use standard data definitions or ones supplied by a host.

sections.title: Beads and Data Structures
sections.content:
The proposal calls its smallest referenceable data units beads. Beads are built from fields and can be combined into larger structures. A bead has a fixed length and an unambiguous structure; a standard set is available in standard mode, while users may define additional beads in extended mode.

The proposal describes two standard structure types. VECTOR represents sequences such as strings, arrays, and tables. PLEX represents directed graphs, trees, and rings. Control fields describe such details as links between beads and the types or environment associated with them.
sections.plainLanguage: A bead is the smallest data item the proposal can reference. Larger structures are made by linking beads into sequences or graph-like forms.

sections.title: Host-Specific Translation
sections.content:
The proposal places a “generator” in each host. The generator accepts rules describing the host's data structures and environment, then creates a translator between the host's representation and the Network Machine representation.

The RFC presents this as a way for programs written in different languages to communicate when their data structures can be described in NIL. It also discusses the possibility of implementing translation in hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host would describe its own data formats to a generator. The generator would create a translator between those formats and the Network Machine format.
